issues.issue: "Securities" is defined circularly as "securities or other assets", leaving the class of assets that may be repo'd hereunder without an ascertainable boundary. The trailing "unless otherwise agreed in writing" also leaves open which oral agreements escape the Agreement's governance.

The definition strings enumerated insolvency events against open-ended catch-alls — "or similar law", "similar official", "an order having a similar effect" — so the reach of each catch-all beyond the listed specifics is contestable. Whether a given filing is an Act of Insolvency matters because 11(a) makes the default self-executing.

The fallback percentage is computed from "Market Value" on the Purchase Date, a term itself dependent on a contested pricing source, and the clause never says how an "agreed" percentage must be evidenced. Whether a margin percentage was ever agreed for a Transaction is therefore open.

The deadline defaults to whatever is "established in accordance with market practice" whenever the parties have not fixed one, and neither Annex I nor Annex II fixes one here. That leaves the cut-off for same-day margin satisfaction, on which Paragraph 4(c) and Event of Default (iii) turn, to be proved rather than read.

"Market Value" turns on a price "obtained from a generally recognized source agreed to by the parties" and is qualified by "unless contrary to market practice for such Securities", none of which is defined; for illiquid mortgage securities the price so obtained is genuinely contestable. The whole margin machinery in Paragraph 4 and the Event of Default in 11(iii) depend on this figure.

Annex I paragraph 7 supplants the "source agreed to by the parties" with Telerate/Reuters/Bloomberg and, failing those, with Buyer's own affiliate, which sits awkwardly against this definition's bilateral-agreement premise. A court would have to decide which controls the valuation.

The definition points to "the prime rate of U.S. commercial banks as published in The Wall Street fournal", a garbled source name, and gives no fallback if no such rate is published. It matters only for default interest under 11(h).

The opening quotation mark is missing from the second sentence's "Purchased Securities", a typographical slip that does not change meaning but does show the definition's edges were not policed. Whether substituted or additional securities remain "Purchased Securities" after a default is the live question.

The Repurchase Price accrues to "the date of such determination", which Paragraph 11(f) then caps for a defaulting Buyer while 11(a) deems the Repurchase Date to occur immediately; fixing the determination date after a default requires reading these together. That interaction is a plausible point of construction.

Permitting a Transaction to be "made orally" leaves the existence and terms of a Transaction to be proved by testimony rather than text. Which oral exchange constituted the agreement is a classic construction fight.

The Confirmation is "conclusive evidence" unless "specific objection is made promptly after receipt", and "promptly" is given no measure. That window decides whether a disputed Confirmation term binds.

The last sentence gives this Agreement priority over a conflicting Confirmation, while Annex I paragraph 3 amends that very sentence to give the Confirmation priority; the unamended text remains in the instrument. A court asked which document governs a conflicting trade term would have to reconcile the two.

Demand must be made "no later than such time as is customary in accordance with market practice", an unfixed benchmark that determines whether a termination demand was timely. Nothing in Annex I supplies the customary time.

The Margin Deficit is measured by "aggregate Market Value", a contested input, and the cure may be made in "additional Securities reasonably acceptable to Buyer", a standard the Buyer applies to itself. Whether a margin call was validly made and validly refused turns on both phrases.

The transfer deadline is keyed to the "Margin Notice Deadline" and to "the close of business in the relevant market", neither of which is fixed anywhere in this instrument. Whether a margin transfer was late — an Event of Default under 11(iii) — cannot be answered from the text alone.
Attribution of cash is left to what "shall be agreed upon by Buyer and Seller", with no default rule if they never agree. In a wind-up that gap decides which Transaction the cash reduces.

Buyer's election between crediting Income and applying it is left to what "Buyer shall reasonably determine in its discretion", combining a reasonableness standard with unfettered discretion. The carve-outs (A) and (B) then suspend the obligation on Buyer's own view that a Margin Deficit would result.

The paragraph simultaneously asserts the Transactions are sales "and not loans" and deems a pledge "in the event any such Transactions are deemed to be loans", so its operation depends on a characterisation the clause itself disclaims. Which regime governs the parties' rights to the securities is the question.

Annex I paragraph 8's replacement Paragraph 12 grants each party an outright security interest in all property transferred, without the "deemed to be loans" condition this paragraph imposes. The two grants cannot easily be read together.

Segregation is required only "[t]o the extent required by applicable law", leaving the obligation's content to be supplied from outside the document. The same paragraph then permits Buyer to rehypothecate freely.

The statement that "[a]ll of Seller's interest in the Purchased Securities shall pass to Buyer on the Purchase Date" sits against Paragraph 6, which contemplates that the same Transactions may be deemed loans secured by a pledge from Seller. Full passage of title and a retained pledgor interest are hard to harmonise.

The disclosure is left with its drafting alternatives unresolved — "they [will]* [may]** be subject to liens granted by Seller to [its clearing bank] [third parties]**" — so the parties never chose between materially different statements. A reader cannot tell which version was adopted.

Substitution here requires Buyer's agreement and acceptance, while Annex I paragraph 11 inserts a 9(c) giving Seller a unilateral right to substitute subject only to Buyer's election to refuse. The relationship between the consent regime and the notice regime needs reconciling.

Representation (v) sweeps in violation of "any law, ordinance, charter, by-law or rule" or "any agreement by which it is bound", an unbounded catch-all repeated on every Purchase Date. Because 11(vi) makes an incorrect representation an Event of Default, the reach of that list carries real weight.

The trigger list is closed and uses undefined qualifiers — a representation "incorrect or untrue in any material respect", and clause (iv)'s misprinted cross-reference to "Paragraph S" — so whether a given event is an Event of Default is contestable. Only clause (iv) carries a notice/cure step, leaving the others self-executing by negative implication.

Annex I paragraph 8's replacement Paragraph 12 makes a default under any other agreement between the parties an "Event of Default hereunder", enlarging a list this paragraph presents as exhaustive. A court would have to decide whether the enumeration is closed.

The option is "deemed to have been exercised immediately" on an Act of Insolvency yet elsewhere must be declared, and notice need only be given "as promptly as practicable", so the effective default date is uncertain. That date drives the Repurchase Price and every valuation under 11(d).

The liquidation remedy is governed by "in a recognized market (or otherwise in a commercially reasonable manner) at such price or prices as the nondefaulting party may reasonably deem satisfactory", and by a deemed price "obtained from a generally recognized source" chosen "in its sole discretion". Whether a liquidation was commercially reasonable and correctly priced is exactly what these words leave open.

Sub-paragraph (e) lets the nondefaulting party fix the pricing source "[u]nless otherwise provided in Annex I", while Annex I paragraph 7 prescribes Telerate/Reuters/Bloomberg with a CSFB affiliate fallback for Market Value. Which pricing regime applies to a default liquidation must be construed.

Clause (iii) is a catch-all for "any other loss, damage, cost or expense directly arising or resulting from" a default, sitting after two specific heads of recovery, so its reach beyond replacement and hedge costs is uncertain. "Directly arising" is itself the boundary term.

Annex I paragraph 13 bars liability "UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES" for indirect, incidental, special or consequential loss, while this paragraph allows recovery of hedge-termination costs and a general residual head of damages. The overlap between the two has to be resolved.

Preserving "any rights otherwise available to it under any other agreement or applicable law" is hard to square with Annex I paragraph 13's absolute bar on consequential and punitive damages. A nondefaulting party could invoke this to escape that cap.

Annex I paragraph 8 states that "Paragraph 12 of the Agreement shall be deleted in its entirety" and substitutes a broader single-agreement and setoff provision, so this text remains in the instrument though displaced. Which version governs setoff and cross-default is a question a court could be asked.

Notices "may" be given by any of several means and "[a]ll notices, demands and requests hereunder may be made orally, to be confirmed promptly in writing", so the clause prescribes no mandatory method and no consequence for failing to confirm. Whether an oral margin call or default notice was effective turns on this.

The clause supersedes only prior agreements "containing general terms and conditions for repurchase transactions", a qualified formula that is not a true integration clause and leaves other prior dealings untouched. Which earlier documents survive is left open.

Annex I paragraph 15 states that this Agreement "covers all Transactions in effect as of the date hereof between the parties", which pulls pre-existing trades into the new terms that this supersession clause addresses only obliquely. The two provisions have to be read together to know what survived.

Treating every provision as "separate and independent" is in tension with Paragraph 12 and Annex I paragraph 8, which declare all Transactions and agreements a single, indivisible business relationship. A party invoking severability against netting would raise that tension.

Termination is by written notice yet "this Agreement shall, notwithstanding such notice, remain applicable to any Transactions then outstanding", so termination has no practical effect while trades remain open. What termination accomplishes, and when the relationship actually ends, is left unclear.

Requiring every modification and waiver to be "in writing and duly executed by both of the parties" sits against Paragraph 13, which permits notices, demands and requests to be made orally, and against Paragraph 3(a)'s oral Transactions. Whether a course of oral dealing altered margin practice would engage that conflict.

"[N]o material adverse change in Seller's financial condition" is a deemed representation with no defined measure of materiality, and 11(vi) turns any untrue representation into an Event of Default. The trigger is therefore judgment-laden.

The preamble recites a Master Repurchase Agreement "dated as of September 20, 1997" while the Agreement it supplements is dated as of September 20, 1998 — a date error going to which instrument the Annex attaches to. It also omits a comma before "the provisions", though that is harmless.

The Annex's blanket priority over conflicting provisions of the Agreement must be squared with Annex I paragraph 3's separate rule that a Confirmation prevails over the Agreement, producing a three-tier hierarchy nowhere fully stated. Ranking Agreement, Annex and Confirmation is left to construction.

This states flatly that all Transactions are sales and purchases, while Paragraph 6 provides for a deemed pledge and security interest if they are instead deemed loans, and Annex I paragraph 8 grants a security interest outright. The characterisation of the trades is left genuinely unsettled across these provisions.

This amended sentence gives a Confirmation priority over the Agreement, the exact reverse of the last sentence of Paragraph 3(b), which remains in the printed instrument. A dispute over a Confirmation term inconsistent with the Agreement would require choosing between them.

The default-interest sentence invokes "the LIBOR Rate" and "the third Business Day", neither of which is defined anywhere in the Agreement or Annex I. The rate and the start date for accrual therefore cannot be fixed from the text.

The forfeiture is triggered by failure to perform "any tax covenant provided for hereunder", with the covenant itself qualified by "reasonably satisfactory" and "reasonably requested". Whether a tax form was adequate enough to preserve gross-up rights is left to argument.

The Tax Event notice is "treated as a demand pursuant to paragraph 3(c)", but 3(c) governs only Transactions terminable upon demand, so its application to a fixed-term Transaction is not provided for. Fixing the effective Repurchase Date for a fixed-term trade requires reconciling the two.

Limb (ii) turns on "a substantial likelihood" that an additional amount will be payable, a threshold with no defined content, and the three limbs are misnumbered with two labelled "(ii)". Either feature makes the trigger for unilateral early termination contestable.

The clause uses "Defaulting Party" as a capitalised defined term, but the Agreement defines only a lower-case "defaulting party" in Paragraph 11, so the indemnity's trigger has no defined referent. The scope of the enforcement-costs indemnity depends on it.
"[A]ny stamp, registration, documentation or similar tax" ends in a catch-all whose reach beyond the three enumerated charges is undefined. The indemnity in 5(e) rides on that boundary.

The eligibility restriction operates "[n]otwithstanding any provision contained in this Agreement or in any additional terms or conditions contained in the Confirmation", which cuts against Annex I paragraph 3's rule that a Confirmation prevails over the Agreement. Which override wins for an ineligible security is unresolved.

Confirmation is assigned to CSFB Corporation as Agent, whereas Paragraph 3(b) requires "Buyer or Seller (or both), as shall be agreed" to deliver the Confirmation. Whose confirmation counts as the operative one is a point of construction.

The Agent is made responsible for issuing confirmations "in compliance with Rule 15c3-1", the net capital rule, where the confirmation rule is Rule 10b-10; the cross-reference does not match the duty described. "Rule [5a-6" is likewise misrendered.

The fallback makes Buyer's own affiliate — "CREDIT SUISSE FIRST BOSTON (HONG KONG) LIMITED or one of its affiliates" — the pricing source whenever "a price is not available" from the three named services, with no test for unavailability. This one-sided allocation of the valuation power is what a valuation dispute would be fought over.

It displaces Paragraph 2(j)'s requirement of a "generally recognized source agreed to by the parties" for Market Value, and its relationship to Paragraph 11(d)'s separate pricing regime for default liquidations is not stated. Which source governs which calculation must be construed.

The replacement Paragraph 12 extends the single-relationship premise to "all transactions and agreements between them", not merely Transactions hereunder as original Paragraph 12 provided, and the superseded text remains printed in the instrument. The scope of the single-agreement concept is therefore contestable.

The setoff right reaches "any other amounts or obligations owing in respect of any other agreement or transaction whatsoever", an unbounded formula with no enumerated limits. Whether obligations unconnected with repo trading fall within it is exactly what "whatsoever" leaves open.

The grant covers property transferred "pursuant to this Agreement or otherwise", and the enforcement route cites "Paragraph 11(d)()" with an empty sub-reference. Both the collateral pool and the enforcement mechanism are left indeterminate.

An outright grant of a security interest in all transferred securities is difficult to reconcile with Paragraph 6 and Annex I paragraph 2, which state that Transactions are sales and purchases and create a pledge only if they are deemed loans. The characterisation of the transfers is left inconsistent.

The notice must be given "at or prior to 10:00 am (New York Time) on such business day", but the only business day previously mentioned is the one this sentence excludes, so the operative day has no antecedent. The timing of a valid substitution notice cannot be fixed from the words.

The unilateral substitution right sits against Paragraph 9(a), under which substitution requires Buyer's "agreement with and acceptance", and against 9(b)'s deemed acceptance for Seller-custody trades. Which consent regime applies to a given Transaction requires harmonising the three.

The amount payable is whatever Buyer's "actual cost" plus a loss figure "solely determined and calculated by Buyer in good faith" comes to, with no methodology and no verification right for Seller. Both the components and the good-faith constraint invite argument.

The absolute bar on "INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL OR CONSEQUENTIAL" loss cannot easily be squared with Paragraph 11(g), which expressly makes a defaulting party liable for hedge-termination costs and any other loss arising from an Event of Default. A damages claim after default would put the two directly against each other.

The clause submits to "EXCLUSIVE JURISDICTION" yet only "SOLELY FOR THE PURPOSE OF" enforcement suits, so whether it forecloses proceedings elsewhere is genuinely open. Exclusivity and a purpose-limited submission pull in different directions.

The single sentence says the Agreement "covers all Transactions in effect as of the date hereof" without saying whether it displaces the terms on which those trades were originally struck. Retroactive coverage of open trades is left unexplained.

It must be read with Paragraph 14, which supersedes only prior agreements "containing general terms and conditions for repurchase transactions", leaving the status of trade-specific prior terms for existing Transactions unresolved. The two together do not say what governs an open pre-existing trade.
